extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of moral philosophy (Aristotle's Ethics)
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of Aristotelian criteria for Happiness and Human Excellence (virtue): what counts as happiness, how virtues arise and are characterized, the role of pleasures/pains, the mean between excess and defect, and requirements (external goods, complete life).

rubrics_metrics.name: Happiness as activity of the soul in perfect excellence
rubrics_metrics.description: "Happiness belongs to the class of things precious and final... since Happiness is a kind of working of the soul in the way of perfect Excellence."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Happiness is not a mere feeling or transient good but an activity (operation) of the soul performed in accordance with complete (perfect) excellence. The text repeatedly frames Happiness as the chief good and final end (the starting-point toward which actions aim).

rubrics_metrics.name: Happiness determined by virtuous workings, not by changes of fortune
rubrics_metrics.description: "To make our sentence dependent on the changes of fortune, is no way right: for not in them stands the well, or the ill, but... the workings in the way of virtue are what determine Happiness."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fortunes (good/bad external events) are accessories; they do not in themselves determine whether a life is happy. A truly good person bears external changes nobly; small fortunes don't affect the balance of life, great misfortunes may, but virtue is primary. Examples: good general/shoemaker doing best with what he has; noble bearing of mischance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of sufficient external goods and a complete life (and fitting death)
rubrics_metrics.description: A happy man must "work in the way of perfect virtue, and is furnished with external goods sufficient for acting his part in the drama of life... during a complete life" and "his death must be in keeping with such life."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle allows that some external goods are necessary to perform virtuous activities (e.g., enough property, health, friends). Happiness requires not a brief fortunate interval but a complete life of virtuous activity; an untimely or dishonorable death can undermine claiming full happiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Goods of descendants/friends affect the dead only trivially
rubrics_metrics.description: On whether the fortunes of descendants/friends contribute to the condition of the dead: if anything reaches them it must be "something trivial and small... neither to make happy them that are not so otherwise, nor to deprive of their blessedness them that are."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle argues against large moral import of others' fortunes on a dead person's blessedness; only minor goods/ills could 'pierce the veil.' This sets a limit on considering posthumous fortunes as part of a person's happiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Happiness is a final, precious end (not a faculty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Happiness "belongs to the class of things precious and final. And it seems to be so also because of its being a starting-point... with a view to it we all do everything else that is done."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes happiness from faculties or praise-worthy traits; it is the ultimate end to which actions are directed, comparable to how gods are called blessed. This orients evaluative judgments toward ends rather than mere faculties or praise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of Excellence: Intellectual vs Moral
rubrics_metrics.description: "The Excellence of Man then is divided... we make two classes, calling the one Intellectual, and the other Moral; pure science, intelligence, and practical wisdom — Intellectual: liberality, and perfected self-mastery — Moral."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intellectual virtues (e.g., science, intelligence, practical wisdom) mainly arise from teaching and time; moral virtues (e.g., temperance, courage, liberality) arise from habituation/custom. Any account of human excellence must distinguish these origins and forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtues arise by habituation (action precedes state)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The Virtues then come to be in us neither by nature... but we are furnished by nature with a capacity for receiving them, and are perfected in them through custom... by doing just actions we come to be just; by doing the actions of self-mastery we come to be perfected in self-mastery; and by doing brave actions brave."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Virtue formation requires repeated practice/actions; mere talk or knowledge is insufficient. Lawgivers and educators aim to produce virtue by habituating correct actions in citizens. Anti-patterns: assuming virtue comes automatically from nature or merely from theoretical knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possession of virtue requires right inner state beyond mere action
rubrics_metrics.description: One must not merely perform right acts; to possess a virtue one must do them "knowing what he is doing, next if with deliberate preference, and with such preference for the things' own sake; and thirdly if being himself stable and unapt to change."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle distinguishes producing right outcomes (as in arts) from being virtuous: virtues require the agent's correct motivational state, deliberation, and stability. Example anti-pattern: producing a correct act by chance or under compulsion does not make one virtuous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue concerns pleasures and pains (education should train proper responses)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Moral Virtue has for its object-matter pleasures and pains... by reason of pleasure we do what is bad, and by reason of pain decline doing what is right... men should have been trained straight from their childhood to receive pleasure and pain from proper objects."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral education must shape what we take pleasure/pain in so that our responses incline us to right action. Virtues are states relating to feelings and actions where pleasure and pain indicate formation of habit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test of formed habits: pleasure or pain following the act
rubrics_metrics.description: "For a test of the formation of the habits we must take the pleasure or pain which succeeds the acts; for he is perfected in Self-Mastery who not only abstains... but is glad to do so; whereas he who abstains but is sorry to do it has not Self-Mastery: he again is brave who stands up against danger, either with positive pleasure or at least without any pain; whereas he who does it with pain is not brave."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the subject's affective response after acting as an indicator of genuine habituation: taking joy in the virtuous abstention or acting without painful reluctance signals genuine virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue is a state (not feeling or capacity)
rubrics_metrics.description: "By Feelings... Capacities... States... the virtues... must belong to one of the three classes... Since then the virtues are neither Feelings nor Capacities, it remains that they must be States."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle classifies virtues as stable dispositions ('states') that determine relations to feelings (too much, too little, or the mean). This distinguishes virtues from transient emotions (feelings) or mere abilities (capacities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of the mean: virtue is a mean between excess and defect (relative to the agent)
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is the nature of such things to be spoiled by defect and excess... the mean state preserves [virtue]." "The exactly equal is a mean between excess and defect... by the mean relatively to ourselves... that which is neither too much nor too little for the particular individual."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Virtue requires finding the mean between extremes of excess and deficiency. The mean is relative to the individual's circumstances and capacities (not an absolute arithmetical middle). Examples: courage avoids both cowardice (defect) and rashness (excess); self-mastery avoids both licentiousness and insensibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Habits and subsequent actions reciprocally reinforce each other
rubrics_metrics.description: "Not only do the origination, growth, and marring of the habits come from the same circumstances, but also the acts of working after the habits are formed will be exercised on the same... by abstaining from pleasures we come to be perfected in Self-Mastery, but when we have come to be so we can best abstain from them."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is a reciprocal relationship: practice forms habit; formed habit enables better future practice. This circular reinforcement supports progressive moral development and proficiency in virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral reasoning admits of outline, not exact rules for particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: "All which can be said on moral action must be said in outline... matters of moral action and expediency have no fixedness any more than matters of health... it must be left in each instance to the individual agents to look to the exigencies of the particular case."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One should not expect precise formulaic rules for every moral situation; ethical judgment requires practical wisdom (phronesis) to apply general principles to particulars, similar to medicine or navigation.
